messages.subject: Parsimonious and intermediate solutions
parts:
Dear Professors and QCA Researchers, 

Thank you very much in advance for your help. 
I have a few questions about interpreting and reporting the parsimonious and intermediate solutions. 

Currently, my sample has 480 cases. I set the incl. cut = 0.85, pri. cut = 0.65, and n. cut = 3. This sample is used to compare with another analysis, which has only 198 cases. I used the same incl. cut and pri. cut but the n. cut was 2 there in the smaller sample. 

Question 1: Is a condition considered “core” if (a) it appears in both the parsimonious and intermediate solutions or (b) so long as it appears in parsimonious solution?

The situation is: I have terms in the QCA-PS that does not seem to be a superset of any QCA-IS (please see example below), what should I do?
  • QCA-PS: A*B*~F + B*E*I +....(there are others)
  • QCA-IS:  A*B*~D +  B*E*I + B*E~D+A*B*C~F*E... (there are more)
  • As in, there are more terms in QCA-PS but the closest to the second and third term in QCA-IS is B*E*I already; 
  • I assumed the last term in QCA-IS can be "matched" with the first term in QCA-PS but I am not sure what to do with the A*B*~D
Relatedly, question 2,  if a term in the QCA-PS is not a superset of any of the QCA-IS, is it recommended to take away that term in the model (but keep the rest that works?) Or is the whole solution not valid and there are other things I should check?

I am trying to present my results using the chart suggested by Prof. Peer Fiss and I wonder (question 3): When I report the overall solution in chart, are the overall solution consistency and coverage scores taken from the intermediate solution? 

I am sorry if my questions are stupid. 
Thank you very much in advance for your guidance. 


Yours faithfully, 
Esther

messages.author: 53dbab5845ace6b6
messages.subject: Re: [QCA] Parsimonious and intermediate solutions
parts:
Dear Esther,

The parsimonius solution term A*B*~F is indeed a superset of the intermediate solution term A*B*C~F*E.
All individual elements: A, B and ~F are present in the configuration A*B*C~F*E.

This is what makes, for instance, a hypothetical A*B a superset of A*B*C

Does this solve your question?
Adrian

messages.author: 53dbab5845ace6b6
messages.subject: Re: [QCA] Parsimonious and intermediate solutions
parts:
Hi Esther,

A set can be a superset of itself.
That is, if you have a parsimonious term (say) A*B, and an intermediate term still A*B that is not problematic. It still means the parsimonious solution is a superset of the intermediate solution, because A*B can be considered a superset of A*B.

Hope this helps,
Adrian

messages.author: 53dbab5845ace6b6
messages.subject: Re: [QCA] Parsimonious and intermediate solutions
parts:
Dear Esther,

It would help a lot preparing a minimal reproducible example. In principle, the intermediate solution is in-between the conservative and parsimonious solutions, in the middle of the so-called complexity - parsimony continuum.

The very procedure to derive the intermediate solution makes sure the PS is a superset of the IS, please have a look at the original paper by Ragin and Sonnett, as well as in my QCA workshop presentation:
https://zenodo.org/records/10396802

I hope this helps,
Adrian
